title: LLM Judges Can Be Too Generous When There's No Reference Answer
hook: Grade without an answer key and an LLM judge tends to wave wrong answers through — hand it the reference, and up to 85% of those verdicts flip to incorrect.
key_points: Reference-free LLM judges systematically over-credit incorrect answers as correct, across the three languages tested.
Adding the reference answer to the judge's prompt flips its correct/incorrect verdict by up to 85% in some settings.
Reference-driven flips generally align with human annotations — the reference-aware version is the more trustworthy one.
Two-stage pipeline: calibration tests judge task knowledge; sensitivity tests reference presence/positioning effects.
Takeaway: calibrate LLM judges with reference-aware evaluation before trusting them in reference-free setups.
content_html: LLM-as-a-judge is now a routine way to grade open-ended model answers, often without a ground-truth reference to check against. Kranti and Vajjala test whether that reference-free setup is actually reliable, running judge models through a two-stage pipeline across three languages. The short answer: no — judges tend to let incorrect answers slide as correct when there's nothing to compare against.
extra_html: The first stage, calibration experiments, probes whether the judge model even knows enough about the task it's grading. The second, sensitivity experiments, tests how much the judge's verdict shifts when a reference answer is added to the prompt, and where it's placed. Across the languages studied, adding the reference flipped the judge's correct/incorrect call by as much as 85% in some settings — and those reference-informed verdicts lined up much better with a subset of human annotations than the original reference-free ones did. The authors frame this as a blueprint: before deploying an LLM judge in a reference-free setting, calibrate it first with reference-aware evaluation. Chalamalasetti Kranti and Sowmya Vajjala, arXiv 2026 (arxiv.org/abs/2607.12885).

related.title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate?
related.hook: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes evaluation is easier than generation — a controlled test finds the opposite on 3 of 4 benchmarks, and attention analysis shows why.

flashcards.prompt: What happens when an LLM judge evaluates answers with no reference answer available?
flashcards.back_html: It tends to over-credit incorrect answers as correct — a bias the authors found consistently across the three languages they tested.

flashcards.prompt: What did adding a reference answer to the judge's prompt do to its verdicts?

choices.text: Flipped correct/incorrect verdicts by as much as 85% in some settings
Made the judge harsher on correct answers too

flashcards.explanation_html: Reference presence and position had large sensitivity effects — and those flips tracked human judgments better than the reference-free verdicts did.

flashcards.prompt: What two-stage method do the authors propose for trusting an LLM judge in reference-free settings?
flashcards.back_html: Calibration experiments check the judge's own task knowledge; sensitivity experiments check how reference presence/position shifts its verdicts.
